Theme

root noun

of a plant

also roots, take root, put down roots, by the roots, pull up by the roots

classical

Cato Agr. 28.1: bene cum rādīcibus eximitō
Cic. Off. 2.43: rādīcēs agit

rādīx, rādīcis f.

noun, third declension

a root

Mostly in the plural for a plant’s roots: rādīcēs agere or capere, “to take root” (Varro, Cato), ab rādīcibus, “by the roots” (Caesar). Also the root of the tongue or of a hair, the foot of a mountain (sub rādīce montis, Cato Agr. 1.3), and an edible root, especially the radish (Lewis & Short). The root of a matter is fōns or orīgō (see source).

Other words

  • stirps, stirpis f. — the stock: the lower trunk with its roots

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Liv. 21.36.1: virgulta ac stirpēs circā ēminentēs

    The base of a plant, roots and all, and so a young plant or shrub; figuratively a family’s stock or lineage (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • cum serēs, bene cum rādīcibus eximitō cum terrā suā quam plūrimā circumligātōque, utī ferre possīs

    when you transplant it, lift it out well with its roots and as much of its own soil as you can, and tie it round so that you can carry itCato Agr. 28.1

  • vēra glōria rādīcēs agit atque etiam prōpāgātur, ficta omnia celeriter tamquam flōsculī dēcidunt

    true glory puts down roots and even spreads; everything false quickly drops, like little blossomsCic. Off. 2.43

  • trūditur ē siccō rādīx oleāgina lignō

    an olive root pushes out of the dry woodVerg. G. 2.31

See also tree, source, sow.
